html:
A burst of speculation in tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic that peaked and collapsed in February 1637. It is often called the first speculative bubble.

Tulips came to Europe from the Ottoman Empire in the 1500s and became a luxury flower. The most prized were "broken" tulips with flame streaks, caused, as we now know, by a virus. Rare bulbs such as the Semper Augustus sold for huge sums.

In the winter of 1636 to 1637 traders in taverns bought and sold contracts for bulbs still in the ground, often with no money changing hands. Prices for even common bulbs shot up, and in early February buyers suddenly stopped appearing. Prices crashed and courts refused to enforce many contracts.

The story was made famous by Charles Mackay in 1841. Modern historians think the damage was smaller than he claimed, and the Amsterdam economy carried on. But the tale is still told in every later bubble, from the South Sea scheme to dot com shares.
sum: A burst of speculation in tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic that peaked and collapsed in February 1637. It is often called the first speculative bubble.
